The line “My doggy hoodied, got online and skrrt the Wraith like Ralph” by Lil Yachty in the song “Boat Interlude” contains some elements of slang and wordplay. Let’s break it down:

“My doggy hoodied”: “Doggy” is a slang term that is often used to refer to a close friend or someone you trust. “Hoodied” likely means wearing a hoodie. So, the line could imply that Lil Yachty’s friend or associate, who he trusts like a “doggy,” is wearing a hoodie.
“Got online”: This suggests that Lil Yachty’s friend went online, possibly referring to accessing the internet or social media platforms.
“Skrrt the Wraith like Ralph”: “Skrrt” is an onomatopoeic term often used in hip-hop to imitate the sound of tires screeching. “The Wraith” is a luxury car made by Rolls-Royce. “Ralph” could be a reference to the fashion brand Ralph Lauren, known for its association with luxury and high-end lifestyle.
Therefore, the line as a whole could mean that Lil Yachty’s trusted friend, who was wearing a hoodie, went online and drove a luxurious car (the Wraith) in a way that symbolizes wealth and success, similar to the lifestyle often associated with Ralph Lauren. The use of “skrrt” adds a sense of excitement and energy to the description.

meaning:
Katy compares sonic distortion to media distortion, i.e. inaccuracy or lies from biased news sources. People who are compelled by the propaganda are lulled into a false sense of security, just like music compels them to dance. Rather than thinking critically, they’d rather mindlessly distract themselves, as though they were zombified.

https://twitter.com/katyperry/status/827637139781201921

“We think we’re free” could be a reference to Donald Trump’s proposed and enacted laws, like banning refugees from multiple Muslim-majority countries from entering the United States and defunding Planned Parenthood. These actions provide the illusion of a freedom, but actually make it more selective—some are free, but only at the cost of others' rights.

In a broader sense, the line could refer to the way we stereotype others and micromanage our own behavior. We think we’re free because we’re told we are, but how many of us actually take advantage of that opportunity? Freedom is a choice, and Katy wants people to be more aware of that.

line: So put your rose-colored glasses on And party on
vault_lines: So put your rose-colored glasses on
meaning:
Double Meaning




First meaning: 
Coloured or tinted lenses reflect various different concepts (no pun intended). On one end of the spectrum, there is the general cliche of the symbolic rose-tinted spectacles which means sugar-coating, or reality-denying. Someone who sees the world through “rose-colored glasses” believes it’s more pleasant than it actually is, and potentially ignores critical events happening around the world that challenge their idealism.

Therefore, this line would portray Katy Perry’s distaste towards those attempting to cover their shallow-mindedness with their glam-ed physical appearance “Air, look so good”. In Katy’s eyes, society underestimates its problems. She encourages this ignorance in a tongue-in-cheek fashion because partying is more comfortable than realizing the world’s troubles.



On the other side, sunglasses physically have a connotation to the “LA Girl” – the concept of a materialistic, superficial female who parties away her life without care for the deeper meaning of life. And party on"

Second meaning: 

Katy Perry may also be alluding to the red retina obtained from smoking weed – hence, putting “rose-coloured glasses” on, “and party on”.

meaning:
Perry is referring to the wealthy part of society that purposefully separates themselves from others through things like gated communities. They are “trapped in [their] white picket fence.” She is illustrating how they make what seems like a perfect world, “utopia”.

When she asks when will it be enough, she’s pointing out that the top 1% of society keeps getting richer and richer, for seemingly no reason.



Perry has a point when she questions the loneliness of the rich—the richest people in America have a highly increased rate of suicide and loneliness is one of the leading causes of suicide.

After the 2016 presidential election, many media outlets blamed the surprise win of Donald Trump on media bubbles. It became such a widely discussed issue that President Obama mentioned it in his farewell address.

For too many of us, it’s become safer to retreat into our own bubbles, whether in our neighborhoods or college campuses or places of worship or our social media feeds, surrounded by people who look like us and share the same political outlook and never challenge our assumptions. The rise of naked partisanship, increasing economic and regional stratification, the splintering of our media into a channel for every taste – all this makes this great sorting seem natural, even inevitable.

Katy’s lyrics reflect Obama’s main concern; we live in bubbles where everyone shares the same opinion as us. Until we leave the bubble and “climb into [someone’s] skin and walk around in it,” we remain oblivious to the troubles of our fellow Americans.

meaning: The verse, on the surface, appears to be a collection of aggressive, high-energy flexes, but when analyzed through the lens of DC2Trill’s absurdist worldview, it becomes clear that these words are intentionally devoid of concrete meaning—an extension of his identity as a “Drank Baby”, the title of his album and a concept deeply rooted in the culture of intoxicated detachment. A “Drank Baby” is someone raised in the haze of lean (codeine mixed with soda), where perception is warped, time is fluid, and language itself loses coherence. This forms a surrealist collage, where meaning is irrelevant, and only momentary sensation matters. Much like Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, this verse exists in a realm where communication is stripped of logic, existing solely for rhythm, sound, and fleeting impact. DC2Trill, by rapping in this fragmented, almost nonsensical manner, exposes the emptiness of a world where excess and intoxication reign supreme. The “Drank Baby” is not just a persona—it is a state of being, where language itself dissolves under the weight of perpetual inebriation, leaving behind only aesthetic echoes of meaning, drifting like smoke in a styrofoam cup.

line: Touch screen on my toaster
vault_lines: Touch screen on my toaster
meaning: The lyric “Touch screen on my toaster” is more than just a flex—it is a profound critique of excess, power, and the illusion of control, echoing Shakespeare’s Macbeth. Just as Macbeth blindly trusts the witches’ prophecies, believing himself untouchable, the rapper flaunts wealth that ultimately does nothing to change the fundamental nature of life—much like how a touch screen does not alter a toaster’s core function. This line subtly mocks the fallacy of invincibility, exposing how materialism only amplifies inner emptiness, much like Macbeth’s doomed kingship. It also serves as a veiled diss toward Drake, who, in the ongoing Kendrick Lamar conflict, is often criticized for his opulent yet hollow persona—luxurious but disconnected, rich yet lacking true authenticity. The toaster represents technological excess, just as Drake represents commercial excess, while the touch screen, a frivolous addition, mirrors how Drake’s industry dominance feels increasingly artificial. Just as Macbeth’s castle crumbles despite his power, so too does the illusion of security in both wealth and rap supremacy—proving that, in the end, anybody can get touched.

line: Durag on my head, it’s The Boonies
vault_lines: Durag on my head, it's The Boonies
meaning:
“The boonies” is a slang term for the literal definition of “boondocks,” which refers to an isolated, rural, and usually considered unsophisticated area of living.

Due to the subject matter of this line, that being durags—headwear typically seen as representing African-American culture—as well as the context from the previous line about movies, “the boonies” presumably refers to the American comic strip The Boondocks and its anime-inspired animated sitcom adaptation created by Aaron McGruder for Adult Swim in 2005. The show typically incorporates racial stereotypes and generalizations, such as Black people wearing durags, into its humor. Boat uses the show’s subject matter to describe his fashion sense.

This line is not the first time Yachty mentions The Boondocks, releasing an entire song about the character Riley Freeman in 2018 as track three of Nuthin' 2 Prove. It is also not the only instance of a hip-hop song referring to the television show as “The Boonies,” as Killer Mike and The Alchemist have a collaboration from 2014 titled “Boonies (The Boondocks).”

A year later, he’s branded himself as the “King of the Youth” with two #1 rap hits and as one of the most heavily influential popular musicians of 2017.

line: Top the charts, Hip Hop ain’t the same we the new stars Rock stars,
vault_lines: Top the charts, Hip Hop ain’t the same we the new stars
meaning:
Almost abruptly, the entire hip hop scene changed in late 2016-17. New rappers came with rock influences, and punk-influenced rap songs began dominating the charts, with “XO Tour Llif3” spending nearly six months in the top 2 of Spotify and genre blurring act XXXTentacion gaining hundreds of millions of streams since debut “Look At Me!” hit the Top 40. Since 2017, nearly all breakout artists in hip hop have deliberately distanced themselves from the existing “old head” culture in some way or another.

But it’s also how rappers see themselves in culture and style what contributes to their “rockstar” image. A rapper’s lifestyle with parties, drugs, women and money, all common themes in contemporary rap lyrics, is very reminiscent of the rockstar lifestyle stereotype of the 70’s/80’s which brings to mind personalities like Jimi Hendrix or Keith Richards.

Lil Yachty topped the rap charts in the US for one week with “iSpy” and for nine weeks with “Broccoli” in addition to topping the R&B charts. His debut album, Teenage Emotions debuted in the T5 of the Billboard 200 and at #3 on the rap charts.

Additionally, this is a reference to Kanye’s famous Yeezus interview with BBC where he references himself as the #1 “rock star” on the planet and calls hip hop the new rock culture. It’s also the inspiration for a video created by Genius about how rappers are the new rockstars.

line: Paint dripping like I’m whipping marmalade (whoa)
vault_lines: Paint dripping like I’m whipping marmalade (whoa)
meaning:
In English-speaking countries,  marmalade is a citrus fruit preserve that comes from oranges, typically boiled with water and sugar to make jam. It’s thick enough that it might resemble the consistency of paint while dripping out of the jar.

However the original “marmalade” wouldn’t drip at all, as it is a firm and sticky reddish quince paste, often in a brick-like shape. The term originates from the Portuguese word for quince, “marmelo.” Its jam, called “marmelada,” was exported to England from the Iberian Peninsula as early as the 15th century.

Though it’s unclear when oranges were first used to make a preserve with that name, in Britain “marmalade” became solely associated with an orange or citrus preserve, and in many European countries it became a generic term for fruit preserves. In Portugal, it’s still only the quince paste.

line: Double R parked right outside like a raisin in the sun
vault_lines: Double R parked right outside like a raisin in the sun
meaning:
Simile that compares a “double R” to “a raisin in the sun” via how it is “parked.” “Double R” refers to a Rolls Royce, while “raisin in the sun” invokes both a line from Langston Hughes' 1951 poem “Harlem”:


What happens to a dream deferred?

Does it dry up
like a raisin in the sun?
Or fester like a sore—
And then run?
Does it stink like rotten meat?
Or crust and sugar over—
      like a syrupy sweet?

Maybe it just sags
      like a heavy load.

Or does it explode?


along with the title of Lorraine Hansberry’s 1959 play, A Raisin in the Sun, which itself draws on Hughes' poem for her title.

Both the poem and the play engage the question of “What happens to a dream deferred?,” respectively in New York City and Chicago. Their commentary offers a critique of the “double R” that starts the simile, for while the person owning it may have made it, the implication is that this success came at the cost of the community where it is parked, invoking the poem’s own “dry up like a raisin in the sun” comparison to clarify impact of the “double R” here.

Lil Yachty references A$AP Ferg’s hit song “Plain Jane,” flipping the original chorus:

Ferg is the name, Ben Baller did the chain
Tourneau for the watch, presi Plain Jane

A$AP Ferg broke down what this line meant on the song page for “Plain Jane”, during an interview with Genius Lyrics, and said:

“Plain Jane” means when you ain’t got no diamonds or nothing in it. This represents class to me without all of the diamonds and everything in it. It does have baguettes on the inside of it. When you keep it plain Jane, or OG or somebody that’s very classic, they be like, “Oh, yeah, he didn’t …” You kept the stock rims on your car, that’s what it’s like. You didn’t have to throw the spinners and all of the trinkets on it to make it stand out. You ruin a watch that way. It’s like you buy a car and you just fuck it up with everything else. You buy it stock and keep it that way. The only diamonds that you’ll see on my watch is the ones that come with the watch.

Although Ferg is hesitant to add anything to his watch, Yachty is eager to “flood his” with as many diamonds as he can.

In addition to this, “Plain Jane” appeared on Ferg’s album, which is entitled Still Striving and actually featured Yachty on the track “Aww Yeah.” The two have collaborated numerous times before and have remained friends over the years.

meaning:
Lil Yachty is poking fun at his detractors who claim that he is a member of the up and coming class of “mumble rappers”, who rap with minimal lyrical substance and utilize extremely repetitive topics and subject matter.

This line is most likely a direct response to Wiz Khalifa who recently called out Yachty for being a mumble rapper. In an interview with Hot 97, Ebro, one of the hosts, asked Khalifa about his opinion of Lil Yachty and Lil Uzi Vert, and Wiz responded by saying:

“We call it mumble rap. It ain’t no disrespect to the lil homies, they don’t want to rap. It’s cool for now, it’s going to evolve. Those artists, if they want to stay around, they’ll figure out the next thing to do. But right now, that’s what’s poppin.”

Lil Yachty was also a member of the XXL Freshman Cypher class of 2016, along with rappers such as Denzel Curry, 21 Savage, Lil Uzi Vert, and Kodak Black. Many people consider this class one of the worst ever, due to their use of “mumble rap”.

This drill a wave, a vicious tide
meaning:
“A bunch of youngins tryna slip and slide”
Sauce describes younger people jumping into drill culture. “Slip and slide” works as wordplay: on one hand, it’s playful (like the children’s water toy), but in the drill context it can mean moving recklessly, sliding on opps, or trying to gain clout without fully understanding the risks.

“This drill a wave, a vicious tide”
Drill is framed as a cultural wave, something trendy and irresistible that everyone wants to ride. But calling it a “vicious tide” adds darker weight: waves can be fun, but tides can pull you under.

The line suggests drills are both exciting and dangerous, with consequences for youngins / newcomers that might not be ready for.

meaning:
Juice WRLD’s Drug Use 

Juice had made it public that he had large issues with drug abuse, especially lean and Percocets, and said that if it caused him issues in his relationship with Ally Lotti, he was willing to let it go.

In the posthumously released track Wishing Well from the album Legends Never Die which honored Juice’s legacy, he touches more on his drug addiction, stating:

Let’s be for real
If it wasn’t for the pills, I wouldn’t be here
But if I keep taking these pills, I won’t be here, yeah
I just told y'all my secret, yeah
It’s tearing me to pieces
I really think I need them
I stopped taking the drugs and now the drugs take me

In another posthumously released track titled No Good Juice exclaims more on how he know the drugs ruin his image as a public figure:

Using opiates overly, openly fuckin' up my image, yeah





Methamphetamine, also called meth or crystal meth, is a highly addictive stimulant drug. It gives a temporary feeling of energy and happiness, but can have serious negative effects on physical and mental health.

Long-term use can cause dental problems, skin sores, weight loss, insomnia, paranoia, and other issues. It is illegal and considered dangerous due to its high potential for abuse and addiction.





Vicodin is a brand name for a prescription medication that contains two active ingredients: hydrocodone and acetaminophen. It belongs to a class of drugs called opioids, which are pain relievers.

Long-term or excessive use of Vicodin can lead to physical dependence and addiction. Abruptly stopping the medication after prolonged use may result in withdrawal symptoms. Common side effects include drowsiness and nausea.





Percocet is a strong prescription painkiller that contains two main ingredients: oxycodone, which is an opioid, and acetaminophen, a common pain reliever.

It is typically prescribed for moderate to severe pain relief, such as after surgery or for chronic pain conditions. However, Percocet carries a risk of addiction and misuse. It can cause side effects like drowsiness and constipation.

meaning:
This is a quote from the American half-hour instructional television show, The Joy of Painting, which is hosted by legendary painter, Bob Ross. The host often gifts meaningful life advice to the watchers, alongside tips on how to become a seasoned artist, as he relates his paintings to experiences he has gone through.

This sample is from season one, episode one titled “A Walk in the Woods," where Bob is seen painting a “happy little tree” as he demonstrates to everyone to start in an artistic world.

An inspirational message from Bob Ross at the end of the track can allude to how Yachty allows his thoughts to run its course freely. In the construction of this album—which is distinctly different from his previous albums since his 2021 mixtape, BIRTHDAY MIX 6—he zoned directly into an experimental and fresh tone era, which contains many weeks of planning in all the prototype of the album and its finish.

Yachty had previously spoken about wanting to switch up his music in an interview with Complex, on January 10, 2022, stating:

I’ve always wanted to [make an alternative album] but now I’ve met all these amazing musicians and producers […] It’s like a psychedelic alternative project. It’s different. It’s all live instrumentation […] I’ve changed my dynamic […] I’m creating music a whole lot differently.

meaning:
Yachty refers to the ubiquitous Quentin Tarantino, one of the most iconic film directors of the 21st century. He’s known for his deep filmography of classic movies including Kill Bill, Pulp Fiction, and Django Unchained.



Quentin Tarantino.

Tarantino’s movies are primarily marked by their gripping dialogue, unorthodox storytelling, and provocative scenes. Yachty feels that love is uniquely chaotic in a similar way.

It’s worth noting that love is a driving force behind a couple of Tarantino’s most popular movies, such as Kill Bill where the main character seeks homicidal revenge on an ex lover or Jackie Brown where the titular character outsmarts the antagonist due to her affair with one of his business partners.

line: Sex symbol, the Black Seminole A sex symbol, the Black Seminole
vault_lines: A sex symbol, the Black Seminole
meaning:
The Black Seminoles, also referred to as Afro-Seminoles, Seminole Maroons or Seminole Freedman, were a group of American runaway slaves that joined forces with the Seminole Indians in present day Florida and Oklahoma from the 1700’s to the 1850’s.



A portrait of John Horse (1812-1882) of the Black Seminole people. Horse was notably of mixed ancestry, being both African and Indian.

The Black Seminoles fought alongside the Native Seminole people in the Seminole Wars (1817-1858.) Many Black Seminoles like John Horse (pictured above) were functionally “head generals,” as they led their men into battle during these wars.

In saying “sex symbol,” it’s possible that Yachty is referring to the fetishization of darker skinned people. This is arguably most prevalent with Black Americans, but is commonly imposed on Indigenous people as well. Through phenomena like this, Black and other non-European cultures are often reduced to entertainment for White, western audiences to enjoy in their media, i.e., “on every channel.”

Yachty could possibly be using the story of the Black Seminole as a metaphor for venturing into new territory with his music. At the listening party for the album on January 27th, 2023, Yachty claimed that part of his reason for departing from his usual sound on this album was to be taken seriously as an artist:

I think I created it just because I really wanted to be taken serious as an artist, you know. Not just some SoundCloud rapper, not some mumble rapper. Not some guy that just made one hit.

In the same way that Black Seminoles escaped slavery to create a new culture, Yachty sees himself escaping the “SoundCloud rapper” label to create a new sound of psychedelic rock.
